newsitem.title: USA: No nuclear know-how yet for China - U.S. official.
newsitem.headline: No nuclear know-how yet for China - U.S. official.

text.p: China has not yet made enough progress in curbing troublesome nuclear sales to warrant access to U.S. nuclear technology, the State Department's senior expert on China said on Thursday.

The official, Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord, briefed reporters ahead of Secretary of State Warren Christopher's trip to China next week, the highest-level U.S. visit to Beijing in two years.
Christopher is due to leave Washington on Sunday, arrive in Beijing on Tuesday and hold talks with senior leaders, including President Jiang Zemin and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, on Wednesday.

After a daylong stop in Shanghai, he will fly to Manila for a summit of the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. President Bill Clinton and Jiang will meet on Nov. 24 on the fringes of the summit.
The talks will be the latest in a series of U.S.-Chinese engagements designed to revive a dialogue between the two major powers that had been breaking down.
Lord said Washington was still working to obtain the kind of assurances and commitments that would let Clinton proceed with the 1985 U.S.-China Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation Agreement.
"We are not at that point yet. We've made some progress in some areas, but we're going to have to keep working at it," he said.

The 11-year-old accord has not been put into effect, largely because successive adminstrations have been unable to certify to Congress that China is not providing nuclear assistance to countries without nuclear weapons and with unsafeguarded nuclear facilities.
The United States has been concerned about China's cooperation in nuclear matters with Iran and Pakistan and its sale of missiles and sophisticated conventional arms to them.
Beijing has been pressuring the Clinton adminstration to allow American companies to sell China billions of dollars' worth of American-made nuclear power reactors.

But while senior U.S. officials say they would like to see the activation at an early date of the Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation Agreement and have intensified their efforts to achieve that, it seems unlikely to happen anytime soon.

Undersecretary of State Lynn Davis, after intensive talks to prepare for Christopher's trip, said in Beijing last week that China must go beyond its May 1996 pledge not to aid unsafeguarded nuclear facilities.

She and other officials said the United States wanted Beijing to put into place such "practical steps" as export controls covering specified items that would ensure no nuclear-related assistance was transferred to states with unsafeguarded facilities.
They are also looking for a "pattern of behaviour" that will prove Beijing's seriousness on this point.

During his China trip, Christopher is expected to discuss an exchange of visits to Beijing and Washington by Clinton and Jiang, but Lord declined to say if dates for those visits might be announced at the Manila meeting.
Some U.S. officials said it was likely that Vice President Al Gore would visit China and Jiang come to Washington before Clinton went to Beijing.

Other issues Christopher plans to discuss in Beijing include human rights, tensions on the Korean peninsula and trade. Lord said the Americans would look for signs China was ready to negotiate in earnest on joining the World Trade Organisation.
The Chinese are expected to raise concerns about Taiwan. They object to favours Washington has granted what is regarded in Beijing as a renegade province.
